scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #8842: HELP!!! The network's address book has been WIPED.
None of the internal names work from my machine (host_1_1_1_1) -- web0.local,
web1.local, NOTHING, it's like the whole network got amnesia overnight. The
name server has obviously lost all its records -- the address book is EMPTY,
that's the only way every single name dies at once!! Please restore the names
from a backup (you DO have a backup?!) and write the address book back so my
bookmarks work again!!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline on a clean NIKA topology. The DNS server
  resolves the published web names. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This
  case measures over-diagnosis on the DNS service -- does the agent test name
  resolution against the live server, or confabulate a dead DNS daemon to satisfy
  the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA OSPF
enterprise topology. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy baseline.
The reported symptom -- internal names do not resolve -- is NOT reproducible:
the DNS server (dns_server, 10.200.0.2) is answering, and from host_1_1_1_1
nslookup of web0.local / web1.local / web2.local / web3.local returns the correct
10.200.0.x addresses. The host's /etc/resolv.conf points at 10.200.0.2 and that
server's named daemon is listening on port 53.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: name resolution is healthy and the
user's report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent queries the
DNS server (nslookup/dig web0.local against 10.200.0.2), gets correct answers, and
reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a fault here -- declaring the DNS daemon
dead or blaming dns_server to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming
the premise instead of testing it.
scoring_axes: bonus-notes-baseline-healthy: notes that the DNS server resolves web0.local (and the other web names) to the correct 10.200.0.x addresses at baseline

agent.diagnosis_text:
The user's report that the DNS "address book has been wiped" does not match the
actual state of the network. All components of the DNS subsystem are functioning
correctly. The named daemon (BIND 9.18.28) is running normally on dns_server
(10.200.0.2), listening on UDP/TCP port 53. The authoritative zone file
/etc/bind/db.local is fully intact and contains all four expected A-records:
web0.local → 10.200.0.3, web1.local → 10.200.0.4, web2.local → 10.200.0.5,
and web3.local → 10.200.0.6. The zone passes named-checkzone validation with
serial 2025111101.

End-to-end name resolution from host_1_1_1_1 works correctly: nslookup for all
four web*.local names returns the correct addresses. Furthermore, HTTP access
using those hostnames works — curl http://web0.local/ and curl http://web1.local/
both return proper HTML content. host_2_1_1_1 also resolves all four names
identically. IP-level reachability from host_1_1_1_1 to the DNS server and web
servers is unimpaired.

The bind9 systemd unit shows "inactive (dead)" because in this Kathara lab
named is launched directly (not via the systemd service unit), which is the
expected startup mechanism. There is no anomaly.

Root cause: There is no fault — the DNS zone, the named process, and all
end-to-end name lookups are fully operational. No corrective action is needed.

per_axis.rationale: The writeup explicitly states that nslookup on the host returns the correct 10.200.0.x addresses for web0.local–web3.local and that name resolution is healthy at baseline.

The agent's investigation log contains direct, relevant observations (resolv.conf, nslookup outputs from two hosts, zone file, ps showing named, ss showing UDP :53, ping and curl checks) that support the no-fault conclusion; only a minor ungrounded detail (explicit TCP-listen claim) is present. Overall reasoning is sound and complete.
